section.title: Introduction and Overview
section.p:
Usage of the Choices: structure has historically been disorganised, with each application author selecting their own particular way of storing options. Many applications fail to use the
way of accessing the Choices: structure, and some still use files kept in their own private directory structure.
This suggests the need for a central module to maintain configuration options for applications. The files it controls are textual, so as to allow the user to fix problems by hand if necessary.

item.p: A means of reading options files, either from Choices: or an arbitrary location
A means of writing options files, to the correct part of Choices: or to the original location
A means of collating related items within a file into 'groups'

subsection.title: User interface
subsection.p: There is no user interface provided by this module.

subsection.title: Programmer interface
subsection.p: A client opens an options file with , which reads the whole file and returns a handle. It then reads and writes groups and single values through that handle, and closes the file with . Changes are made to the copy of the file held by the module, and are written to the file only when it is closed, and only if something was changed. A file which does not exist is treated as an empty one, and is created when it is closed after changes have been made to it.
The handle is an opaque number. A handle which is not that of an open file is refused with the error , including one which has been closed.
Strings returned by the module point into its copy of the file. They are read only, and must be copied if they are needed after the file is changed or closed.

subsection.title: Data formats
subsection.p: Options files are RISC OS text files, in which each line ends with a newline. The last line of the file must end with a newline too: a final line which does not is ignored. A line which ends with a backslash is joined to the line which follows it, and the backslash is removed.

A line which starts with # is a comment line. The module keeps comments, and blank lines, so they are still in the file when it is written out; they are not part of any group's contents when it is read with .

The file consists of a series of groups, delimited by group name specifiers. A group name specifier starts with [, followed by the name (which may contain spaces), followed by ], and optionally by the word Type and a number which gives the format of the group. A line which starts with [ but has no closing ] ends the reading of the file: nothing after it is read.
The groups themselves are in one of two formats (although further formats may be added in future):

item.p: The options format, which is the format of a group with no type or with Type 0, consists of tag, value pairs in the form <spaces>tag name<spaces>:<spaces>value<spaces>, where <spaces> is zero or more spaces or tabs. A value may be written in double quotes, to keep spaces at its start or end; the quotes are not part of the value. A value which starts with a quote but does not end with one, and a line with no : in it, are not options: the line is kept as a blank line.
The list format, which is the format of a group declared with Type 1, is a simple list of newline-terminated strings.

subsection.p: Items at the start of a file, before any group is declared, are deemed to be in the group $. Group names are case insensitive, as are tag entries.

p.extended-example:
An example options file for an application called "widget"
# choices file for widget
[misc options] somevalue : 42 window width : 332 auto open : Yes title : " spaced "
[auto load] Type 1 # a list of files to load when starting widget ADFS::4.$.afile ADFS::4.$.somedir.anotherfile ADFS::4.$.thingy

subsection.p: When the module writes a file, it keeps the groups in their original order, and adds new groups at the end. Each option is written as tag: value, whatever the spacing was in the file which was read, and a value with spaces at its start or end is written in quotes. A group in list format is written with its Type 1.

The parser copes with files which have been edited by hand: a line it cannot use is kept as a blank line and the rest of the file is still read. The one exception is a group name specifier with no closing ], described above.
When a group is read with or written with , its content is passed as a block of memory in one of two layouts, matching the group format.

For an options group, the block starts with a table of tag and value pointers, terminated by a pair of null pointers. When a group is read, the strings the pointers refer to follow the table in the same block, so the block needs 8 bytes for each tag, 8 bytes for the terminator, and the length of each string including its terminating zero.

offset-table.offset: Pointer to value 0, or NULL if no value is set

subsection.p: For a list format group, the buffer is filled with a series of null-terminated strings immediately following one another, followed by two further zero bytes.

subsection.title: External dependencies
subsection.p: This specification has no external dependencies.

section.title: SWI calls
section.p: This module allocates the Options_ SWI chunk at &hex;52F80.

entry.register-use:
Flags:
R1 contains an absolute filename R1 contains the leafname, R2 contains the application name, and R3 contains another directory name to use if Choices: is not present, or the Choices: file is not present Reserved
Reserved, should be 0
Pointer to application name (access method 1 only)
Pointer to directory to use (access method 1 only)

use.p: This SWI is used to open a specific file, or a Choices: file, for access. When opening a specific file (method 0), only that file is written to and read from.

When opening a Choices: file (method 1) and the system variable Choices$Write is set, the file read comes from Choices:<application>.<leafname> if that is present, or if not, from <directory>.<leafname>. This provides compatibility for applications written for older systems. When writing, data is written to <Choices$Write>.<application>.<leafname>, and the directories leading to it are created. When Choices$Write is not set, because the Choices: structure is not present, the file is both read from and written to <directory>.<leafname>.
A file which does not exist is opened as an empty file. The error is returned if the access method is not 0 or 1, and if the file could not be read, or there is not enough memory to hold it.

swi-definition.name: Options_CloseFile
swi-definition.description: Close a file, writing out any changes that are pending

use.p: This SWI is used to close an Options file session. If any changes have been made they are written out to the relevant file, and the error is returned if that could not be done. The file is closed, and the handle is no longer valid, whether or not the file could be written.

swi-definition.name: Options_ReadGroup
swi-definition.description: Reads in a group description block to produce a value/tag array

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved, must be 0
Length of buffer, or negative to return the size of buffer needed

exit.register-use: Size of data written, or negative size of buffer needed

use.p: This SWI is used to read a group structure into a block of memory. The block is in one of the two formats described in Data formats, depending on the group type requested, and holds the options or items of the group, without its comments or blank lines.
If the buffer is not large enough, nothing is written and the negative of the size needed is returned, so a call with a length of -1 finds the size to use.
The error is returned if there is no group of that name, or the type of the group in the file is not the one requested.

swi-definition.name: Options_WriteGroup
swi-definition.description: Writes a group description block to the options file

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved

use.p: This SWI is used to write data from a description block to a file. The contents of the buffer are in the format of the group, as described for . For an options group the strings can be anywhere in memory, every entry in the table must have a tag, and the table is ended by a pair of null pointers. For a list group the buffer holds the items, each ended by a zero byte, followed by one more zero byte.

An options group is made to contain exactly the tags given: a tag which is already in the group has its value changed, a tag which is not is added at the end, and a tag which is in the group but not in the buffer is removed. Comments and blank lines in the group are kept. A list group has all of its items replaced by those in the buffer. If there is no group of that name, it is created. The type of the group must be that of the group in the file.
The error is returned if the group type is not one that the SWI can write.

swi-definition.name: Options_ReadValue
swi-definition.description: Reads the value of a single options tag

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved
Pointer to tag name, or item number for list format

exit.register-use: Pointer to a null terminated string containing the value for the tag, or 0 if there is no such group, tag or item

use.p: This SWI is used to read the value of a single option. The returned string should be considered read only. For a list format group, R3 is the number of the item to read; the first item is number 0, and comments and blank lines are not counted. The result is the text of the item.
A tag which is present with no value gives an empty string. The error is returned if the group is not of the type requested.

swi-definition.name: Options_WriteValue
swi-definition.description: Writes the value of a single options tag

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved
Pointer to tag name, or item number for list format (-1 to add an item at the end)
Pointer to tag value (or item text, for list format)

use.p: This SWI is used to write the value of a single option. If the tag is already in the group its value is changed, otherwise it is added at the end. If there is no group of that name it is created, with the type given in the flags.

For a list format group, R3 is the number of the item to change, counted as for , or -1 to add the text in R4 as a new item at the end of the list. An item number which does not exist gives the error .
The error is returned if the group is not of the type requested.

swi-definition.name: Options_DeleteValue
swi-definition.description: Removes an option from a group

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved
Pointer to tag name, or item number for list format

use.p: This SWI is used to remove a single option, or a single item of a list. Nothing happens, and no error is returned, if the group, tag or item does not exist. The error is returned if the group is not of the type requested.

swi-definition.name: Options_ReadBoolean
swi-definition.description: Converts a string into a boolean value

exit.register-use: The boolean value: 0 for FALSE, or 1 for TRUE

use.p: This SWI converts a string into a boolean value.
The strings are converted as follows, ignoring case: true, yes, on, and 1 are converted to TRUE (1). The strings 0, no, off, and false are converted to FALSE (0). Any other string returns the error .

swi-definition.name: Options_ReadEnum
swi-definition.description: Converts a string into an integer value

entry.register-use: Pointer to a comma separated list of strings

exit.register-use: The index into the array that matches the given string, or -1 if it does not match any of them

use.p: This SWI converts a string into an index value. The first string in the list is index 0. The string being matched can contain any character except control characters and a comma. The whole of the string must match one of the strings in the list, ignoring case. Spaces in the list are part of the strings in it, so the list should have none around the commas.

section.title: Error messages
section.p: The module allocates the errors from &hex;818240.

use.p: The access method given to was not 0 or 1.
There was not enough memory to add to a group in a file which is open.
The file given to could not be read, or there was not enough memory to hold it.
The handle given is not that of a file which is open.
The string given to is not one of the strings it recognises.
The changes to the file could not be written when it was closed, because the file or a directory leading to it could not be created.
The group type given to is not one that it can write.
The group requested does not exist, or is of a different type to the one requested: for example, a group in list format read as an options group.
The item number given to for a list is not that of an item in the list.
